en.title: Ninja Gaiden
en.summary: Ninja Gaiden is a 2004 action-adventure game developed by Team Ninja and published by Tecmo for the Xbox.

cards.text: Ninja Gaiden is a 2004 action-adventure game developed by Team Ninja and published by Tecmo for the Xbox. A reboot of the Ninja Gaiden franchise, players control Ryu Hayabusa, a master ninja, in his quest to recover a stolen sword and avenge the slaughter of his clan. It is set in the same world as Team Ninja's Dead or Alive fighting games.

Tecmo developed Ninja Gaiden for five years, targeting a western audience. The violence created difficulties obtaining content ratings, and it was censored in some regions. Tecmo promoted Ninja Gaiden international online contests using the Xbox Live service. Record-breaking numbers of players competed for places in the live final held at the 2004 Tokyo Game Show.

Ninja Gaiden received acclaim, with praise for its combat, graphics, and difficulty. It sold more than 1.5 million copies and became one of the ten best-selling Xbox games. It sold 362,441 copies in North America in the first month of release; however, Japanese sales were poor.

Team Ninja released two packs of downloadable content, which were incorporated into a reworked version, Ninja Gaiden Black, in 2005. In 2007, Ninja Gaiden was ported to PlayStation 3 as Ninja Gaiden Sigma, with graphical improvement and gameplay changes; this was released on the portable PlayStation Vita as Ninja Gaiden Sigma Plus. Ninja Gaiden was followed by Ninja Gaiden II (2008), Ninja Gaiden 3 (2012) and Ninja Gaiden 4 (2025). Ninja Gaiden Sigma was released for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, Windows, and Xbox One as part of the Ninja Gaiden: Master Collection on June 10, 2021.

en.title: Custom Robo
en.subtitle: Build a small robot for the next contest
en.summary: Custom Robo is Noise and Studiofake's action role-playing game, first released for GameCube in Japan on 4 March 2004.

cards.heading: Build a small robot for the next contest
cards.text: Custom Robo is Noise and Studiofake's action role-playing game, first released for GameCube in Japan on 4 March 2004. Known there as Custom Robo: Battle Revolution, it became the series' first release outside Japan. Human commanders enter battles through miniature robots, assembling a machine from interchangeable parts before fighting in a virtual Holosseum. A story campaign follows a new commander's encounters and investigations, giving each battle a place in a larger journey while new equipment expands the possibilities for the next match.

cards.heading: Five parts change the same arena
cards.text: The robot consists of a body, gun, bomb, pod and leg parts. Changing them affects movement and the kinds of attacks available, allowing the player to build around a preferred range or tactic. Holosseums vary in shape and can contain hazards such as ice or lava. A configuration that worked in one arena may have difficulty maintaining distance in another. Preparation and direct control therefore remain connected: choosing the equipment establishes the tools, but movement and timing determine whether those tools suit the encounter.

cards.heading: A personal machine inside a larger mystery
cards.text: Outside the arena, the player moves through the human world and speaks to characters who advance the campaign. Inside it, the focus narrows to the selected robot and its opponent. Completing A New Journey opens The Grand Battle, a sequence of tournaments that gives the assembled collection another use. Takayuki Nakamura composed the score. The shift between those scales makes customisation personal: the small machine entering the next Holosseum is the result of decisions made throughout the commander's progress.

en.title: Metal Gear Solid: The Twin Snakes
en.subtitle: Silicon Knights / Konami · GameCube
en.summary: Metal Gear Solid: The Twin Snakes is the GameCube remake of Solid Snake's infiltration of Shadow Moses. Silicon Knights and Konami rebuilt the 1998 PlayStation adventure with new graphics, rerecorded performances and more elaborate cinematics. The nuclear threat, the hostile special forces unit and Snake's uneasy conversations still provide the story, but the player approaches them with abilities introduced in Metal Gear Solid 2. A familiar installation becomes a place whose original arrangement can be investigated through a more capable version of its infiltrator.

cards.heading: Shadow Moses through another generation of hardware
cards.text: Metal Gear Solid: The Twin Snakes is the GameCube remake of Solid Snake's infiltration of Shadow Moses. Silicon Knights and Konami rebuilt the 1998 PlayStation adventure with new graphics, rerecorded performances and more elaborate cinematics. The nuclear threat, the hostile special forces unit and Snake's uneasy conversations still provide the story, but the player approaches them with abilities introduced in Metal Gear Solid 2. A familiar installation becomes a place whose original arrangement can be investigated through a more capable version of its infiltrator.

cards.heading: New tools inside familiar rooms
cards.text: First-person aiming and other expanded actions change how Snake can respond to guards and the surrounding architecture. Enemy behaviour also develops, making communication and detection important parts of a failed approach. The player still needs to observe patrols, use cover and manage what happens after an alarm. Because the locations remain closely related to the earlier game, those extra abilities can substantially change the balance of a known encounter. Returning players may remember the obstacle while discovering that its most useful solution is no longer quite the same.

cards.heading: The same story performed with greater excess
cards.text: Film director Ryuhei Kitamura gave the new cinematics a more extravagant action style, including acrobatics and slowed movement. Much of the English cast returned to record the revised dialogue, connecting the remake to familiar voices even as the staging changed. Released in 2004, the project joined Silicon Knights' experience with Nintendo hardware to Konami's established world. Its identity comes from the meeting of two periods of Metal Gear Solid: the first game's setting and story are played through systems and presentation shaped by what followed.

en.title: Armored Core: Nexus
en.subtitle: Old technology starts another corporate war
en.summary: Armored Core: Nexus is FromSoftware's PlayStation 2 mecha combat game, first released in Japan on 18 March 2004. A corporation's accumulation of ancient technology destabilises the existing powers, drawing the player into missions whose consequences grow increasingly dangerous. The pilot again earns money to alter a personal Armored Core, linking the larger conflict to the machinery used to carry out each contract. Nexus continues the series after Silent Line as a full sequel. Its changes affect how the machine is handled as well as the setting in which the mercenary is asked to work.

cards.heading: Old technology starts another corporate war
cards.text: Armored Core: Nexus is FromSoftware's PlayStation 2 mecha combat game, first released in Japan on 18 March 2004. A corporation's accumulation of ancient technology destabilises the existing powers, drawing the player into missions whose consequences grow increasingly dangerous. The pilot again earns money to alter a personal Armored Core, linking the larger conflict to the machinery used to carry out each contract. Nexus continues the series after Silent Line as a full sequel. Its changes affect how the machine is handled as well as the setting in which the mercenary is asked to work.

cards.heading: Two analogue sticks change the familiar cockpit rhythm
cards.text: Dual-analogue support gives the player a different way to move and aim, updating a control arrangement that had remained distinctive across the earlier games. The underlying task is still to make a customised machine work in a difficult combat situation. Parts, weapons and their interactions need to be considered before the mission, then judged through the response of the machine in motion. LAN multiplayer adds another setting for those designs to meet. The new controls make the familiar systems more immediately accessible without removing the need to understand what the assembled equipment can sustain.

cards.heading: Look back while the series moves forward
cards.text: Rintaro Yamada directed and Toshifumi Nabeshima produced, with Kota Hoshino composing the score. Nexus pairs its new campaign with a second disc revisiting earlier series missions, giving the release both a forward movement and a retrospective element. North America received it in September 2004, with PAL editions following later. The combination makes it a useful point from which to see how Armored Core had developed. Familiar mission ideas can be encountered through revised systems, while the new corporate crisis continues the series' habit of making the mercenary's workshop part of a much larger conflict.

en.title: Katamari Damacy
en.subtitle: The room changes when you grow
en.summary: Katamari Damacy makes growth change the meaning of an ordinary room: what blocks the ball now may become part of it later.

cards.heading: Roll the everyday world
cards.text: Namco released Katamari Damacy for PlayStation 2 in Japan on 18 March 2004. A small Prince must rebuild the stars by rolling a sticky ball through everyday surroundings. Two analogue sticks control its movement, and objects collected along the route become part of the growing mass.

cards.heading: Growth changes a route
cards.text: Size changes the job of the scenery. An object too large to collect can first act as an obstacle, then become useful material once the ball grows. The player revisits the same surroundings with different possibilities, so progress changes how the room is read rather than simply opening another door.

cards.heading: A world with its own musical voice
cards.text: The peculiar royal story and varied vocal music give that repeated action a playful tone. Namco's contemporary announcement presented simple operation alongside strong musical character. The 2018 REROLL edition later renewed the graphics.

en.title: A body becomes a shared toy

cards.heading: A reaction need not be a reward
cards.text: In a 2009 interview conducted with drawing paper and pens, Keita Takahashi questions the assumption that emotion must follow an achieved objective. An animal approaching a camera and looking at it, he suggests, can produce a response without a sequence of completed tasks. He also describes the interest of living beside animals that communicate without human language. These observations connect ordinary life to design. A playful character need not begin as a backstory; how it approaches, looks or reacts can already give someone a reason to care.

cards.heading: Making something within a restriction
cards.text: Takahashi's conversation also turns to restrictions. He says Noby Noby Boy's trophies were a platform requirement rather than something central to his original design. When the interviewers compare creative rules to the impossibility of drawing on the hotel carpet, he draws its pattern on their paper instead. The small gesture makes his point concrete: a limitation can become material for invention. It does not require every constraint to be welcome, but it offers another way to work with what a situation actually permits.

cards.heading: Two players inhabit one body
cards.text: In his own announcement of a Noby Noby Boy multiplayer update, Takahashi describes a peculiar consequence of one BOY eating part of another. The resulting body can have its head controlled by one player and its rear by someone else. With more players, the confusion grows. The rule changes cooperation at the level of movement. People do not simply stand beside one another pursuing separate scores; their inputs can belong to the same awkward creature, making coordination and surprise part of what happens on the screen.

cards.heading: Explaining play is work too
cards.text: The announcement also shows the effort behind presenting such a game publicly. Takahashi recalls preparing for a GDC appearance while travelling from Japan, anxious about whether anyone would want to hear him explain his work. Notes mattered because he could not communicate directly in English. That practical detail sits beside his playful description of multiplayer. An unusual interaction still needs someone to demonstrate and describe it across languages, even when its creator hopes that characters, movement and people's reactions can carry meaning without a conventional plot.

en.title: The Legend of Zelda: Four Swords Adventures
en.summary: The Legend of Zelda: Four Swords Adventures is a 2004 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.

cards.heading: The Legend of Zelda: Four Swords Adventures
cards.text: The Legend of Zelda: Four Swords Adventures is a 2004 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. It is the eleventh installment in The Legend of Zelda series. It was released in 2004 in Japan on March 18, and in North America on June 7. In 2005, the game was released in Europe on January 7, and in Australia on April 7. The Game Boy Advance handheld game console can be used as a controller when using the GameCube – Game Boy Advance link cable bundled with the game in North America and Europe.

cards.heading: Four Links confront Shadow Link
cards.text: Similar to its predecessor Four Swords in terms of gameplay and presentation, the game takes Link and his three clones created by the magic Four Sword on an adventure to restore peace to Hyrule after learning that an evil counterpart of himself, Shadow Link, has been created. Four Swords Adventures was considered the 48th-best game made for a Nintendo system by Nintendo Power, and received an aggregated 86 out of 100 from Metacritic. It was the third best-selling game of June 2004 in North America, with 155,000 units, and has since sold 250,000 copies; it has sold 127,000 units in Japan.

en.title: Far Cry
en.summary: Far Cry is a 2004 first-person shooter video game developed by Crytek and published by Ubisoft.

cards.heading: Far Cry
cards.text: Far Cry is a 2004 first-person shooter video game developed by Crytek and published by Ubisoft. It is the first installment in the Far Cry franchise. Set on a mysterious tropical archipelago, the game follows Jack Carver, a former American special forces operative, as he searches for journalist Valerie Constantine, who accompanied him to the islands but went missing after their boat was destroyed by mercenaries. As Jack explores the islands, he begins to discover the horrific genetic experiments being conducted on the local wildlife and must confront the mad scientist behind them.

cards.heading: CryEngine builds an open-ended battlefield
cards.text: The game was the first to use Crytek's CryEngine, and was designed as an open-ended first-person shooter, though it lacks most of the freedom its successors would offer to the player. While players can freely explore the game's world like in later Far Cry titles, they are most often discouraged from doing so due to the linear structure of missions and the lack of side content. Despite this, the gameplay formula established in Far Cry—placing the player in a foreign environment occupied by enemy forces where they must use various weapons and tools, as well as their surroundings to overcome any threat—would prove essential in defining the series' identity going forward.

cards.heading: A successful debut becomes a series
cards.text: Far Cry was released for Microsoft Windows in March 2004 to generally positive reviews, being praised for its visuals, gameplay mechanics, and the level of freedom given to players. The game was also a commercial success, selling over 730,000 units within four months of release and over 2.5 million units in its lifetime. The success of Far Cry led to a series of standalone sequels developed by Ubisoft, starting with Far Cry 2 in 2008. A remake of the game with a different storyline and new mechanics, Far Cry Instincts, was released for the Xbox in 2005, and for the Xbox 360 in 2006 as part of the Far Cry Instincts: Predator compilation. A loose film adaptation was released in 2008. The original version of Far Cry, updated with HD graphics, was re-released under the title Far Cry Classic for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 in 2014.

en.title: Kirby & the Amazing Mirror
en.summary: Four Kirbies search a connected Mirror World, discovering shortcuts and using a mobile phone to bring their scattered companions together.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: Kirby & the Amazing Mirror is a 2004 platform adventure for Game Boy Advance, developed by Flagship with HAL Laboratory and additional development by Dimps. The series' familiar jumping, floating and copied abilities now serve an interconnected world, while four differently coloured Kirbies can explore it together through Game Link Cable play.

cards.heading: Find a way through the mirrors
cards.text: The shattered mirror gives the adventure its goal: recover the pieces by finding and defeating the bosses hidden across the Mirror World. Doors lead into branching routes, and large switches open mirrors that connect distant areas back to the starting room. A visit can therefore leave something useful behind even when it does not end with a boss. Finding an area map makes its connections easier to understand, while the growing network of shortcuts turns the central room into a practical base for further exploration.

cards.heading: One call brings the others
cards.text: The four Kirbies can go their separate ways. In a solo game the other three act independently; with linked cartridges, friends can make their own discoveries in different parts of the world. Kirby's mobile phone brings them together when help is needed. A call summons the others to his position, giving a difficult encounter or a heavy obstacle a different answer. The battery supply limits repeated calls, so keeping an eye on it matters when setting off down another unfamiliar branch.

cards.heading: The right power for the opening
cards.text: Copied abilities change how Kirby approaches the rooms along a route. Swallowing the right enemy supplies a weapon or movement option; taking damage can knock the ability away and turn recovery into part of the fight. A useful power may be worth carrying beyond the next group of enemies if it opens a passage further on. Treasure chests reward that exploration with maps and other collectibles, making the hunt for mirror pieces share the same spaces with smaller discoveries.

en.title: Mario Golf: Advance Tour
en.subtitle: A golf career begins at the clubhouse
en.summary: Mario Golf: Advance Tour is Camelot's Game Boy Advance sports role-playing game following a young golfer through training, club tournaments and the ambition of eventually playing against Mario. Choosing Neil or Ella supplies the protagonist, with the other character becoming a doubles partner. Exploring the clubs gives the matches a setting beyond the course itself, connecting practice and conversation with a developing sporting career. The handheld adventure gives the player a particular golfer to improve, making the next tournament both a test of control and another stage in that character's progress toward stronger opponents.

cards.heading: A golf career begins at the clubhouse
cards.text: Mario Golf: Advance Tour is Camelot's Game Boy Advance sports role-playing game following a young golfer through training, club tournaments and the ambition of eventually playing against Mario. Choosing Neil or Ella supplies the protagonist, with the other character becoming a doubles partner. Exploring the clubs gives the matches a setting beyond the course itself, connecting practice and conversation with a developing sporting career. The handheld adventure gives the player a particular golfer to improve, making the next tournament both a test of control and another stage in that character's progress toward stronger opponents.

cards.heading: A developing player changes the shot
cards.text: Neil and Ella begin with different strengths in power, precision and shot shape. Training and competition provide ways to develop the chosen golfer, connecting the role-playing structure with the practical decisions made before each stroke. The player still has to read the course and choose an appropriate shot, but the character's capabilities shape what can reliably be attempted. A more ambitious route may become useful as the golfer improves. Development therefore creates new opportunities rather than automatically removing the need to understand the terrain and execute the next swing with care.

cards.heading: Four clubs provide the route toward Mario
cards.text: Marion, Palms, Dunes and Links each offer a course, practice facilities and places where the golfers stay. Winning their tournaments establishes the player's reputation and opens the way toward the larger goal. Moving around these clubs gives the campaign a rhythm of preparation, conversation and competition rather than presenting every match as an isolated menu choice. The connection with Mario's world remains a destination to work toward, allowing the early human cast and its smaller sporting ambitions to occupy a meaningful part of the adventure before the more familiar competitors arrive.

en.title: Pikmin 2
en.summary: Pikmin 2 is a 2004 real-time strategy puzzle video game developed and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.

cards.heading: Pikmin 2
cards.text: Pikmin 2 is a 2004 real-time strategy puzzle video game developed and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. It is the direct sequel to the 2001 game Pikmin and the second game in the Pikmin series. In the game, Captain Olimar returns to the Pikmin planet to collect valuable treasure after learning that the company he works for—Hocotate Freight—is on the verge of bankruptcy.

cards.heading: Two leaders direct the expedition
cards.text: Like its predecessor, Pikmin 2 focuses on exploring an unknown planet's surface from a microscopic perspective, where the player directs the Pikmin to perform various tasks, such as destroying obstacles, defeating enemies, and retrieving objects. It introduces new gameplay mechanics, including the ability to control two different leaders at once and the addition of new Pikmin types.

cards.heading: Reception and legacy
cards.text: Pikmin 2 received critical acclaim, gaining aggregate scores of 89.60% and 90% on GameRankings and Metacritic, respectively. Many critics praised the various additions and changes, such as the new Pikmin types, longer length of the story mode, new multiplayer modes, and the removal of the 30-day time limit imposed in the original game. Pikmin 2 was re-released as part of the New Play Control! series for the Wii in 2009 in Japan, Europe and Australia and it received a North American release three years later in 2012. An HD remaster of the game was released for the Nintendo Switch in June 2023. A sequel to the game, Pikmin 3, was released in 2013 for the Wii U.
